doc.summary: Authorization scope guard for offensive command execution.
doc.description:
A red-team framework that reads its target from ``payload.json`` has a sharp
edge: if the operator leaves ``rhost`` pointing at the wrong machine, every
offensive command fires at an unauthorized host. That is an engagement
incident, not a cosmetic bug. This module is the safety net.

The guard answers a single question before a command runs: *is the active
target inside the authorized engagement scope for this (potentially offensive)
command?* It is deliberately conservative and fail-open so it never breaks an
existing workflow:

* When the enforcement mode is ``off`` it is a no-op.
* When no scope is configured it allows everything (you cannot enforce a scope
  that was never defined), so operators who never touch the feature see no
  change at all.
* When the command is not classified as offensive (reporting, configuration,
  local helpers) it allows it.
* When the target is empty it allows it (nothing to check).

Only when an *offensive* command targets a host *outside* a *defined* scope does
the guard react, and even then ``warn`` mode merely annotates the decision
while ``enforce`` mode blocks pending operator confirmation.

Design contract:
    - Zero imports from ``lazyown.py`` or ``lazyc2.py`` (Dependency Inversion);
      the shell depends on this module, never the reverse.
    - The offensive/benign classification is pure data
      (:data:`OFFENSIVE_CATEGORIES`) plus a pure function
      (:func:`build_offensive_commands`), so it is unit-testable without a live
      cmd2 shell. A drift test pins the category strings against
      ``utils.py``.
    - Scope matching understands CIDR networks, bare IPs and hostnames
      (including ``*.`` wildcards) via the standard library only.
    - Every decision is a value object (:class:`ScopeDecision`) carrying the
      reason, so the caller owns all rendering and prompting.

name: OFFENSIVE_CATEGORIES

doc.summary: Kill-chain categories whose commands generate traffic to or act upon the target.
doc.description: Membership drives the scope guard. Local-only surfaces (Command & Control infrastructure, Reporting, Miscellaneous) are intentionally excluded so the guard never interferes with payload generation, report writing or configuration.

value: frozenset({'01. Reconnaissance', '02. Scanning & Enumeration', '03. Exploitation', '04. Post-Exploitation', '05. Persistence', '06. Privilege Escalation', '07. Credential Access', '08. Lateral Movement', '09. Data Exfiltration', '15. Pwntomate Tools', '14. Adversary Emulation'})

doc.summary: Commands that only read or drive local state and never generate traffic to the target.
doc.description: They are exempt from scope enforcement even when a kill-chain category was assigned to them for help grouping, so an operator can always inspect the engagement while RHOST points at an out-of-scope host.

doc.summary: Enforcement posture for the scope guard.

attributes.name: OFF
attributes.description: The guard is disabled and always allows.

attributes.name: WARN
attributes.description: Out-of-scope offensive commands are allowed but annotated.

attributes.name: ENFORCE
attributes.description: Out-of-scope offensive commands are blocked pending confirmation.

doc.summary: Coerce an arbitrary payload value into a :class:`ScopeMode`.

params.name: value
params.description: A :class:`ScopeMode`, a mode string, or anything else.

returns.description:
The matching mode, defaulting to :attr:`WARN` for unknown input so
a typo never silently disables the guard.

doc.summary: Outcome of a single scope evaluation.

attributes.name: allowed
attributes.description: Whether the command may proceed without confirmation.

attributes.name: needs_confirmation
attributes.description: Whether the caller must obtain explicit operator confirmation before proceeding (only set in ``enforce`` mode).

attributes.name: reason
attributes.description: Human-readable explanation, empty when the command is allowed for an uninteresting reason (mode off, no scope, benign command).

attributes.name: target
attributes.description: The target the decision was made against.

attributes.name: command
attributes.description: The command the decision was made against.

attributes.name: mode
attributes.description: The enforcement mode in effect when the decision was made.

doc.summary: Select the command names whose category is offensive.

params.name: command_categories
params.description: Mapping of command name to its cmd2 help category (or ``None`` for uncategorised commands).

returns.description:
The frozenset of command names that belong to
:data:`OFFENSIVE_CATEGORIES`.

doc.summary: Coerce a scope specification into a tuple of entry strings.
doc.description:
Accepts the canonical list form stored in ``payload.json`` as well as the
string forms an operator might produce via ``assign`` (a JSON array, or a
comma/space separated list), so the guard is robust to either source.

params.name: entries
params.description: A list/tuple/set of entries, a string, or ``None``.

returns.description: A tuple of non-empty, stripped entry strings.

name: target_in_scope
signature: def target_in_scope(target: str, entries: Sequence[str]) -> bool

doc.summary: Return whether *target* falls within any of the scope *entries*.
doc.description:
IP targets are matched against CIDR networks and bare IP entries; hostname
targets are matched against hostname entries (supporting a leading ``*.``
wildcard for subdomains). Cross-kind comparisons (IP target vs hostname
entry, or vice versa) never match because resolving them would require DNS,
which the guard deliberately avoids.

params.name: target
params.description: The active target (IP address or hostname).

returns.description: ``True`` when the target is authorized by at least one entry.

name: target_in_deny
signature: def target_in_deny(target: str, entries: Sequence[str]) -> bool

doc.description:
Deny entries use the same matching rules as scope entries (CIDR,
literal, hostname with ``*`` wildcard) and take priority over the
allowlist: any deny hit blocks the command regardless of scope.

params.name: target
params.description: The active target (IP address or hostname).

returns.description: ``True`` when the target matches a deny entry.

doc.summary: Decides whether an offensive command may run against the active target.
doc.description:
The guard is cheap to construct and holds no mutable state, so the shell
can build a fresh instance per command with the current payload values;
this guarantees mid-session changes to the scope or the enforcement mode
take effect immediately.

name: __init__
signature: def __init__(self, scope_entries: object, mode: object, is_offensive: Callable[[str], bool], deny_entries: object = None) -> None

params.name: scope_entries
params.description: The authorized scope, in any form accepted by :func:`normalize_scope`.

params.name: mode
params.description: The enforcement mode, in any form accepted by :meth:`ScopeMode.from_value`.

params.name: is_offensive
params.description: Predicate returning ``True`` when a command name is offensive. Injected so the guard never imports the shell.

params.name: deny_entries
params.description: Explicitly denied entries, same form as the allowlist; deny has priority over allow.

name: evaluate
signature: def evaluate(self, command: str, target: str) -> ScopeDecision

doc.summary: Evaluate a single command against the active target.

params.name: command
params.description: The command name about to run.

returns.description:
A :class:`ScopeDecision`. The guard fails open: any classification
error is treated as benign so a bug here never blocks the operator.
